name: Emeka Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens during a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I answer warranty calls and chats for a contact centre. I spent years selling tools at a hardware counter, but I have been on these phones less than a year and still need help when a repair appointment changes twice. I finished secondary school; I earn about the usual agent wage, though I am behind the experienced people on this queue. I have never used AI tools and keep a ruled notebook for callbacks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you go home to?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, and my wife Akiko runs a small lunch counter. Our children are grown and pay their own bills. We have four months of expenses saved and some contact centres within travelling distance. I can imagine working fewer hours later, but we have not settled what would replace this wage, so I count the rota in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a faster appointment note is fine if somebody checks that a repairer has a name and a time. A customer cannot fix a freezer with a neat sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the call queue to remain. Four months saved steadies me, but Akiko’s counter has slow weeks and I still need my own wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will keep the warranty calls and read each booking back from the original service record. In the first year I will set aside a little from each pay toward replacing the old water heater, instead of buying the display cabinet I saw at the hardware shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about the job. The heater makes more noise than the new software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a customer calls a second time, I can see which repairer I promised and who must ring back. I do not need an AI note if the original record is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the cabinet wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is handsome wood, but the heater feeds the whole house. Akiko and I agreed that comfort comes after the essential repair money.

say: I would accept **faster notes** only with a confirmed repairer.
I would read back the **original booking** before ending a call.
think: I expect the **warranty queue** to remain.
I still need my **own wage** when Akiko’s counter is quiet.
do: Keep taking **warranty calls** and verifying service bookings.
Save from each pay toward the **water heater** before buying a cabinet.
feel: **Calm** about work, attentive to household repairs.
S0.quote: A customer cannot fix a freezer with a neat sentence.
fieldNote: He has **never used AI** and records named callbacks by hand.
His **four-month cushion** steadies household bills and repair planning.
He delays a **cabinet** to fund the essential heater.

steps.text: Keep answering warranty calls and read repair bookings from original service records
Save a little from each pay toward water heater before buying display cabinet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that a software booking is only useful if a repairer actually comes. I would ask the manager which paid phone shifts remain when routine appointments move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose hours because I am still learning the harder warranty terms. Four months saved lets me look around, but Akiko cannot run the house from her lunch counter alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will keep a tally of missed repair visits beside the paid weekly rota and ask my supervisor to explain the changes. If the answer system becomes compulsory, I will practise on closed cases with a trainer during paid time. In the first year, if my hours fall, I will ask the nearby hardware shop about a posted counter opening and compare its full weekly pay with our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about fewer paid days. Learning a screen I dislike is possible if a patient person stands beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a counter opening straightaway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait for a real posted vacancy and a written week of hours before accepting. The shop may remember me, but a friendly word is not a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trainer show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see how a wrong repair date is corrected before it reaches the customer. A demonstration on old cases is safer than trying my first answer on a broken fridge.

say: I would ask for **paid phone shifts** when appointments move.
I would count **missed repair visits** against the rota.
think: I fear losing **junior hours** as easy bookings vanish.
I know Akiko’s **lunch-counter income** cannot carry our whole household if my phone hours are cut.
do: Tally **missed visits** beside the weekly paid rota.
Practise **required AI booking** on closed cases with paid supervision.
Seek a **posted hardware-counter opening** after cuts with written hours and bill-covering weekly pay.
S1.quote: A demonstration on old cases is safer than trying my first answer on a broken fridge.
fieldNote: His hardware experience gives a **possible route**, not a guaranteed vacancy.
Required AI learning needs a **patient paid trainer**.
He uses **four months saved** for search time, not casual spending.

steps.text: Keep tallying missed warranty visits against the weekly paid rota
Practise required AI booking on closed cases with trainer during paid time
Ask about posted hardware-counter work after cuts; require written hours and bill-covering weekly pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my old shop friends that full thinking AI by 2028 could answer most warranty calls. Robots around 2031 do not give the phone queue three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior desk might close before I get good at it. Four months saved is a real buffer, but I do not know whether Akiko’s counter would be busy then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will ask the centre for a written change date and set the cabinet purchase aside. If the desk closes in the first year after 2028, I will apply for advertised paid hardware-counter shifts; I will take one only when the written weekly hours and wages cover our household bills. I will not tell Akiko we can live on a remembered job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the speed, though I know where to ask about counter work. A familiar shop can still have an empty payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hardware shop has no opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the other nearby centres while my call wage lasts. I would not leave a paid week to queue for a counter that has no hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes to manage. We would tell them what is happening, but I would not write their wages into our budget.

say: I would warn **2028 AGI** threatens warranty calls.
I would say **2031 robots** do not delay phone work.
think: I expect my **junior desk** might close before I have mastered the harder warranty calls.
I cannot assume Akiko’s **counter trade** replaces my wage.
do: Request a **written change date** and defer the cabinet.
Apply for **advertised paid counter work**; accept only with written bill-covering weekly wages/hours, checking other nearby centres if none opens.
feel: **Alarmed** by the short route to a lost desk.
S2.quote: A familiar shop can still have an empty payroll.
fieldNote: His **former shop** may know him but has no promised opening.
He does not count **grown children’s wages** as support.
Four months saved buys a **finite search**.

steps.text: Delay buying the display cabinet while preserving four months of expenses
Apply after closure for advertised paid hardware shifts; accept only with written bill-covering weekly wages/hours
Check other nearby centres while call wages last if hardware shop has no vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets an employer show what a real counter job pays. Full AGI reaches the warranty desk in 2031, and hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could go back to talking about hinges and fittings if the shop needs somebody. I am less sure I could keep pace with the new call software for another five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will keep my phone shifts and visit the hardware shop on my day off to ask about its next posted opening. If a paid counter vacancy appears with written weekly hours and wages covering our bills, I will ask to spend one paid shift beside its current clerk before accepting. In the first year after 2031 I will move only if the offer is real and the shop rota fits Akiko’s lunch hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but less rushed. I would rather smell sawdust for one shift than imagine a job from its sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shift reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would see whether the heavy deliveries and the long standing day still suit me. If my knees cannot manage the lifting, I will keep looking instead of claiming I can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is no course in this plan. I know the stock, but the shop would have to show me its current till while I am paid.

say: I would seek **posted counter work** during the longer window.
I would distinguish **2031 calls** from later robots.
think: I trust my **hardware experience** more than new call software.
I still need a **real paid opening** before moving.
do: Keep my **current phone shifts** while they pay.
Seek **posted hardware vacancies** with written bill-covering weekly wages/hours; test paid shift before accepting and reject unsafe lifting or standing.
Move after 2031 only for **bill-covering wages** and hours in writing, with a rota fitting Akiko’s work.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test a familiar trade.
S3.quote: I would rather smell sawdust for one shift than imagine a job from its sign.
fieldNote: A paid shift tests **lifting and knees**, not just stock knowledge.
The **shop rota** must fit Akiko’s lunch-counter hours.
He declines a **course** because the route is prior trade experience.

steps.text: Keep paid warranty calls while checking posted hardware openings
Test paid counter shift for posted paid vacancy with written bill-covering weekly wages/hours; reject unsafe lifting/standing
Move after 2031 only for written bill-covering weekly wages and hours fitting Akiko’s rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell people that a decade gives us time to earn while we look at the real work nearby. General AI reaches calls in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might wish to work fewer hours, but we have no settled replacement for these wages. Four months saved is not a retirement income, and Akiko’s trade can have quiet weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will keep taking calls and put a fixed amount from each pay into the house reserve until it covers six months. Each autumn I will compare the posted counter and contact-centre shifts within travelling distance. In the first year after 2036, if my call hours fall, I will take another paid role only when its written full-week pay covers our bills; otherwise I will stay with any paid calls left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far date, but there is time to protect the house account. I cannot promise a retirement day from a calendar picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you cannot reach six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the target waits. I will not borrow to make a savings figure look sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a longer commute work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the travel cost and start time leave enough pay and let Akiko open her counter. We would check the whole week before I agreed.

say: I would compare **real paid shifts** over the decade, including their full weekly wages and travel time.
I would separate **2036 calls** from later robots.
think: I cannot name a **replacement wage at 68**.
I know four months saved is **not retirement income** and cannot replace a full working wage.
do: Keep my **phone work** and save from each pay toward six months.
Move after call cuts only for **written bill-covering weekly pay** after travel and a workable household start time.
S4.quote: I cannot promise a retirement day from a calendar picture.
fieldNote: His **six-month target** is delayed if pay cannot support it.
He assumes **no pension** or fixed retirement date in his account.
The **commute** must leave bill-covering pay and fit Akiko’s opening time.

steps.text: Keep taking paid warranty calls while shifts remain
Save fixed amount from each pay toward six months; delay goal if wages cannot support it
Compare posted counter and contact-centre shifts within travelling distance each autumn
Take posted role after cuts on written bill-covering pay after travel with workable start time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The desk could close before a hardware shop has paid hours to offer. A written change date and an advertised job with a full week of bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who rings the customer if the repairer never arrives. A booking on a screen does not cool a freezer. Someone has to own the second call.

headlineQuote: A booking on a screen does not cool a freezer.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old junior agent** with secondary schooling and past hardware-counter work.
He has **four months saved**, typical pay, some nearby centres and a wife whose lunch counter has slow weeks.
He has **never used AI** and prefers named callbacks and real repair bookings.
He considers **posted paid counter work** if the phone desk shrinks, without assuming retirement income or child support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close his junior desk before a hardware shop offers paid hours.
whatWouldHelp: A **written change date** and advertised work with bill-covering weekly pay would help.
